summary: Ages 7-8 compare and order numbers up to 1000 using >, =, < by reasoning from the highest place down: compare hundreds first, then tens, then ones, descending a column only when the current one ties and stopping at the first place where the digits differ. This extends the two-digit 'tens-first' rule to three places. Core practice uses aligned place-value builds with a left-to-right scan, trap pairs (same-hundreds, digit-swap, mixed-length, internal-zero), set ordering, and number-line placement.
misconceptions: Comparing ones or the biggest single digit instead of hundreds first (358 > 372 because 8 > 2).
'More digits = bigger' misapplied, or failing 99 vs 100 by digit count reasoning done wrongly.
Not descending to the next column when the hundreds tie.
Reversing the symbol or binding it to page order.
Ignoring internal zeros when comparing (305 vs 350).

activities.title: Scan the places left-to-right with two aligned builds
steps: Build or view two numbers (e.g. 352 and 358) as aligned base-ten builds or counters in H | T | O columns.
Place a >, =, or < card between them, with the open side facing the larger number.
Work left to right: decide at the hundreds first; only if the hundreds tie, move to the tens; only if the tens tie, move to the ones. Stop at the first place where the digits differ.
Say aloud which place settled the decision and why.
Repeat with trap pairs: same-hundreds (352 vs 358), digit-swap (352 vs 325), and mixed-length (99 vs 100).
Then order a set of 4-5 numbers smallest to largest and place numbers on a 0-1000 number line.
activities.insight: When the numbers are lined up by place, the comparison is always decided at the first (highest) place where the two numbers differ; move down to the next place only on a tie. A bigger ones digit does not by itself make a number larger. A whole number with more digits (and no leading zeros) is larger because it reaches a higher place, as when 100 has a hundred and 99 does not.

activities.title: Consolidation: choose the symbol, order a set, make it true
steps: Choose the correct >, =, or < for pairs including trap cases such as 358 vs 372 and 305 vs 350.
Order a set of five numbers up to 1000 from smallest to largest.
Fill a blank to make a comparison statement true (e.g. choose a tens digit that makes '3_6 > 352' true).
Place a given number on a 0-1000 number line (slider or marked rail).
activities.insight: Fluent, reliable application of hundreds-first comparison across varied pairs and sets, connecting comparison to magnitude on a number line.

activities.title: Annotated worked reference for the scan
steps: Step through a static annotated comparison such as 352 vs 358: see 'hundreds equal → look at the tens → 5 = 5 tie → look at the ones → 8 > 2, so 358 is larger'.
Read the caption that states the rule: compare the highest place first; move down only on a tie; stop at the first place that differs.
Re-state the rule in your own words before trying fresh pairs.
activities.insight: A clear reference model of the left-to-right scan and the stopping condition that learners can return to.

activities.title: Convince-me: rebut a wrong comparison
steps: Respond to a character who claims 358 > 372 'because 8 is bigger than 2'.
Explain why the claim is wrong, using the hundreds-then-tens reasoning, and state the correct comparison.
Construct a short justification: 'Hundreds tie, so look at the tens; 5 < 7, so 358 < 372.'
activities.insight: Being able to justify a comparison in words — not just get the symbol right — strengthens the place-value reasoning behind the procedure.

checkQuestion: Watch them compare and order. 'Put a symbol between 254 and 245. Now order these smallest to largest: 307, 370, 73, 137. Tell me which place you looked at first.' The 254/245 pair turns on the tens, and 73 tests mixing 2- and 3-digit numbers.
checkAnswer: 254 > 245; order 73, 137, 307, 370; comparing hundreds first, then tens, then ones.
